One thing that points to and supports this view is the development of semen in the womb. This would mean that agents with entirely different natures took turns acting on the same matter. That does not happen in natural processes. One agent can hand over the material of its work to another only in deliberate crafts, where the work is done by intention and planning. In nature, the material of each process is bound up with the agent that acts on it.

Just as the natural form perfects bodily matter, plant life is the perfection and end toward which the natural form develops. The truth of this claim is obvious as soon as we consider what “substance” and “accident” mean. One is the negation of the other: an accident exists in a subject, while a substance exists without being in a subject. A thing and its negation cannot both apply to the same thing. By “substance” we mean something whose existence does not depend on a subject; by “accident” we mean something whose existence depends on some subject. So one thing cannot fall under both meanings.

Some ancient thinkers allowed this, though Avicenna thought it unlikely. They offered several arguments. First, the defining features of substances are substances, yet philosophers often call defining features “qualities,” and qualities are accidents. So these defining features would be both substances and accidents.

Avicenna answers that “quality” is used in two different senses here: it is one thing when said of defining features, and another when said of the category of accidents. We can also explain why the defining features of substances are not accidents. As we said earlier, a defining feature does not exist separately from its broader kind except in the mind, when we analyze them. If it were an accident of the broader kind, its existence would have to be separate from the existence of its subject, as an accident’s existence is separate from that of its subject in reality. But the defining feature and broader kind exist as one, since the defining feature is predicated of the broader kind by saying “it is this.” In the mind, where we consider each apart from the other, the defining feature relates to the broader kind as form to matter, not as accident to subject. The defining feature is an intellectual form, and the broader kind is intellectual matter that needs the form in order to become definite and exist. The same is true of the broader kinds and defining features of compounds, though these also differ somewhat in their existence outside the mind: they are matter and form there, not accident and subject.

The fourth argument is this: an accident in a compound is a part of it, so it is not an accident in that compound. Anything that is not an accident in a thing must be a substance in it. The answer is that this argument confuses “substance” with “substantial,” and “accident” with “incidental.” Substance and accident are absolute realities; substantial and incidental describe relations. For example, a human being is a substance in itself and essential to humanity, but incidental to “laughing.” Whiteness is an accident in itself and incidental to the body that receives it, but essential to the compound of body and whiteness. So a thing’s being a part of a compound does not make it a substance in itself. It is a substance only if its essence does not depend on a subject. If its essence depends on a subject, it is an accident, whether or not it is part of something. When philosophers say that a part of a substantial compound is itself a substance, they mean a natural compound with one nature. A part of a natural compound exists in it as matter or form, not as an accident in a subject. Avicenna discusses these points at length in the Categories of The Healing. What we have said is enough for a seeker whose aim is simply to reach what is needed to understand the subject, clear away obstacles, and resist those who mislead—not to master every argument, school, and opinion.
